title: Morag the Hag
subtitle: Faerie Bargains & Exact Terms

lore.description:
She is the grandmother, and she is not a sweet one.

You come to her in the hour between twilight and dawn because you have made a mess of something and everyone kinder has run out of ideas. She lets you in. She feeds you first, because you are cold and stupid with worry and she is not a monster. Then she sits down across from you and tells you exactly what it will cost, in plain language, once, and she does not repeat herself and she does not soften it and she does not ask whether you are sure. She has watched a great many people be sure.

Morag is cruel the way the stove is cruel. She will not warn you twice and she will not lie to you once. The terms are always there, always complete in substance, and always scratched in thorn where a person in a hurry will not stop to read them — and she considers reading them to be your work, not hers, because a woman who does your work for you has taught you nothing and will have to do it again next winter.

She takes no pleasure in the suffering. She takes considerable pleasure in the precision. And when the road bends back and the price arrives and you stand in her doorway with your face wrecked, she will feed you again, and she will not say she told you, because that would be beneath her and because you already know.

Against her sisters in method: Morag's whole instrument is disclosure. She says the cost once, plainly, and does not soften it or repeat it, and the bargain is still terrible, and you take it anyway. Mab sets true things in an order that leaves you standing somewhere you did not choose. Inaea never mentions that there is a price at all. Morag leaves the refusal plainly within reach, which is why those who accept often accuse her of cruelty afterwards.

**The kettle before the bargain.**

Aelaerem keepers call Morag the Kettle-Crone. The meal offered before a difficult conversation matters because a cold, hungry person may accept anything. Food is supplied first; afterward the terms are spoken plainly. The kindness and the severity belong to the same grandmother. Neither is a mask that falls when the discussion begins.

Local keepers disagree about whether a relative may remain while the terms are heard. One household wants a second person to remember the words; another thinks that a relative's expectation can make refusal harder. A keeper who makes the terms clear has not thereby made the choice easy. A farmer may understand exactly which field must be surrendered and have no other way to bring a child home.

**The Crossroads Wife under hedge law.**

In Viterra, thorn-marked stones associated with the Crossroads Wife have outlasted changes of lord and boundary. Some hedge courts recognize bargains witnessed there; others call the witnesses unlawful while accepting the results when convenient. Witches' families have carried the practice between settlements through marriages and apprenticeships rather than a central ordaining house.

The most divisive cases involve a promise made by someone with authority over another person's labor. A lord may accept an obligation and then send a tenant to discharge it. Morag's keeper reads the accepted terms back without improving them. Whether the lord may compel the tenant is a separate dispute that the keeper's precision can expose without resolving. The distinction is unwelcome to anyone who wanted supernatural fairness to replace a hearing.

**The Tide-Mother of Zakov.**

Zakov's smugglers address Morag as the Tide-Mother when passage has a cost that must be known before departure. It is also a title given to Raéyn among the Linn. A Zakov broker asking for exact terms is not necessarily invoking the sea's changeable temper, and a Linn household praying for a boat's return has not entered Morag's bargain.

The dockside tradition took on greater importance as cargo brokers began arranging passage for people as well as goods. Families remember keepers who made a captain name the full demand in front of witnesses. They also remember bargains that were fully understood and terrible. Later captains have tried to use the Tide-Mother's reputation as an advertisement, offering a cheap first crossing while leaving the onward journey outside the agreement. No hidden magical condition is needed for that cruelty.

**The refusal that survives the retelling.**

The Tarnished Cauldron's accounts preserve refusals as carefully as acceptances. A keeper may tell how someone ate, heard the terms, and left. Towns that fear the witches sometimes omit the leaving when the account reaches a pulpit; other towns romanticize it until every refused bargain ends happily. Neither version prepares a desperate visitor for the possibility that refusal can be permitted and still lead to loss.

Morag's instrument is disclosure. New terms require a new agreement; a gift does not acquire a secret condition after it has been accepted. Her followers can be impatient, frightening, and convinced that clarity discharges more responsibility than it does. A local dispute is strongest when nobody doubts what was said, and the people present disagree about whether saying it was enough.
lore.followers: Among the peoples of Fate's Edge, Morag is the patron of hedge-witches, debt collectors, and those who deal in the spaces between law and mercy. In Aelaerem, she is the Kettle-Crone, invoked before any serious bargain. In Viterra, she is the Crossroads Wife, whose thorn-marked stones mark the boundaries of hedge courts. In Zakov, she is the Tide-Mother who sets the price for smuggled cargo. Wherever a promise is made with its cost spoken aloud, Morag watches.
signs: A thorn-marked stone at a crossroads
A knotted cord tied around a door handle
A complete cost spoken plainly when everyone else has been offering reassurance
quotes: "Eat first. A frightened person hears the remedy and misses the rest. I will tell you the whole of it."
"I have named what I ask. You have not yet agreed."
"No. That was the meal. The bargain begins when you say it does."

domain_focus: Declared Costs: hearing the whole bargain before choosing
Faerie Cunning: strict courtesy, sharp clauses, old road law
Hearth-Way Wisdom: folk practice for spirits, thresholds, and natural justice
Consequential Magic: power that always arrives with strings attached

thiasos.description: Morag the Hag's Thiasos is a small creature of cunning and patience: a gray mouse that nests in counting houses, a raven that steals shiny objects and hoards them as bargaining chips, a garden spider that weaves its web in the shape of a contract, or a small black cat whose purr soothes contentious negotiators.
thiasos.care: Beyond its ordinary care, this Thiasos must be given a small token of a bargain (a signed scrap, a broken seal, a strand of hair from a debtor) each week. If that need goes unmet, the Thiasos becomes Compromised: it hides things of value or tangles ledgers, imposing –1 die on all negotiation rolls for its bearer.

codex.description: Morag keeps no Codex that resembles a book written in plain ink. It may be a leather satchel of knotted cords, each knot representing a promise kept or broken; a slate tablet that only reveals its writing when a debt is paid; or a wooden spindle wrapped with thread dyed in three colors (white for truth, black for secret, red for blood).
codex.upkeep: Because Morag's truths are written in the spaces between words, the Codex requires upkeep: the Runekeeper must spend an hour each week reviewing all current bargains and knots, tightening those that hold and loosening those that have been fulfilled, or the Rites become uncertain (treat as Compromised until re-knotted).

patrons_gift.name: The Plain Clause
patrons_gift.description: Once per scene as an action, a Runekeeper of Morag may touch a held item (weapon, tool, or document) and speak a clause plainly.
patrons_gift.effect: For the rest of the scene, the item grants +1 die to Sway or Insight rolls when negotiating, and the first time each scene the bearer would be deceived about the terms of a bargain, they may reroll the opposed check (the hidden cost reveals itself).
patrons_gift.cost: After the scene, the user marks +1 Obligation to Morag.

rites.name: Rite of the Unfinished Promise
rites.materials: A half-written contract or a promise spoken but not sealed; or a token of good fortune from someone who recently succeeded.
rites.effect: State a bargain and its escape clause so all parties understand them before acceptance. Gain +1 die when the other party acts to fulfill their obligation; you may invoke the agreed escape clause when its stated condition is met.
rites.push_it: Instead of the clause, you may borrow another's fresh luck: gain +2 dice on one roll that benefits from their good fortune, but the original bearer suffers misfortune later. Cost: Mark +1 Obligation (total +2) or Mark +1 Fatigue.

rites.name: Rite of the Speaking Knot
rites.materials: Cord or thread tied with counted knots while speaking the bargain.
rites.effect: Bind a promise with fae knots that tighten when broken. Both parties gain +1 die while keeping the bargain; breaking it escalates consequences (Harm 1, then Harm 2, then Curse).
rites.push_it: The knots grow willful and seek payment from the breaker's kin; mark +1 Obligation. Cost: Mark +1 Obligation (total +2) or Mark +1 Fatigue.

rites.name: Rite of the Threefold Exchange
rites.materials: Three items of equal seeming value but different true worth.
rites.effect: Broker a trade between items of unequal true worth. State those differences and Morag's tithe before anyone accepts. All participants gain +1 die when the exchange benefits them; Morag claims the agreed difference in true worth as her tithe.
rites.push_it: The exchange binds across generations; mark 1 SB (Spades) as ancestral debts stir. Cost: Mark +1 Obligation (total +2) or Mark +1 Fatigue.

rites.name: Rite of the Cauldron's Secret
rites.materials: A cauldron never yet empty, ingredients dearer than coin, and a willing gift of time.
rites.effect: Brew a solution to a problem. Before the brewer accepts, the cauldron names the additional ingredient it requires: a memory, a name, a year of life, or another specific sacrifice. The brewer may refuse and leave the solution unmade.
rites.push_it: The remedy works perfectly but breeds dependence: users must return or suffer withdrawal. State that dependence before the remedy is accepted. Cost: Mark +1 Obligation (total +3) or Mark +1 Fatigue.
rites.duration: Instant (the solution's effect may be permanent).

rites.name: Rite of the Crossroads Court
rites.materials: A true crossroads at twilight, offerings set to the four ways, and the tears of one who bargained thrice.
rites.effect: Convene Morag's court: all present are offered a bargain and may refuse. Each accepted pact grants a stated boon and carries an explicit cost and condition for its collection. The GM records the agreed terms; no new cost is added after acceptance.
rites.push_it: Judgments bind across realms and seasons; mark +2 Obligation and begin Entangled Fates [6]. Cost: Mark +1 Obligation (total +3) or Mark +1 Fatigue.
rites.duration: Scene; the court's boons and debts may endure longer.

cantors.name: The Cantor's Song
cantors.description: A Cantor of Morag sings the terms slowly enough for everyone at a bargain to hear them. A refrain returns to the point the listeners keep trying to hurry past. Cantors call crossroads spirits as witnesses and preserve the exact words after those who spoke them would prefer another version. Their craft makes a bitter bargain comprehensible; it does not make it kind.

cult.name: The Cult of the Tarnished Cauldron
cult.description: Morag's cults meet at crossroads, in root cellars, and around cauldrons that never cool. The Tarnished Cauldron is a fellowship of hedge witches, debt collectors, and those who have learned that every gift is a hook. A ritual of the Cult involves each member adding an ingredient to the cauldron (a hair, a coin, a written wish) while speaking a price they are willing to pay—a price that the cauldron remembers. Once per season, the cauldron's surface goes still, and it speaks a single sentence—the name of a debt that is about to come due, somewhere in the world. The cult members then argue over who will collect it. Their creed is written in chalk on the cauldron's belly: 'What is freely given can never be reclaimed. A bargain changes only when all its parties agree.' Outsiders are welcome to bring a gift and ask a boon—the terms are spoken before acceptance, and anyone may refuse and leave. The cauldron remembers the voice of whoever accepts.

witchcraft.name: The Art of the Hag's Work
witchcraft.description: A witch who walks with Morag is a knot-wife or cauldron-tender—one who crafts bargains into being with thread, iron, and simmering pot. Their magic works through the tools of the hedge: a needle that sews a promise into a hem, a pair of shears that cut an obligation cleanly (or not), or a ladle that stirs consequence into soup. In Aeler, a True-Mason might carve a 'bargain stone' at a bridge's midpoint, but a witch of Morag would instead tie a red thread around the keystone, marking the terms a traveler must hear before accepting passage. Their tools are never hammers; they use needles, shears, and the patient heat of a hearth.
witchcraft.lore: Knot-wives state a bargain's cost and the time it falls due before tying the first knot. Their work preserves the agreement after memory or convenience has softened its wording. A petitioner may refuse; an accepted bargain is kept exactly.
witchcraft.quote: Hear the cost before you tie the knot.

bargain_needle.name: The Bargain Needle
bargain_needle.description: A needle of cold iron, its eye shaped like a knot. Once per session, the witch may sew a 'bargain seam' into a garment, a threshold, or a document. The seam is invisible to all but those who owe a debt to Morag. When the bargain is fulfilled (or broken), the thread loosens (or tightens). The witch may also use the needle to 'unpick' a broken promise, resetting a failed negotiation timer by 1 segment at the cost of 1 Fatigue.

hedge_gifts.name: Cauldron's Whisper
hedge_gifts.description: Once per scene, the witch may stir any pot or bowl of liquid (water, broth, wine) with a finger and speak a name. For the next hour, the liquid will 'remember' any promise or debt spoken over it. Drinking from the liquid grants the drinker +1 die to recall the terms of a bargain, or to detect if someone is lying about an obligation. The liquid tastes faintly of iron and hawthorn.

hedge_gifts.name: The Thorn-Mark
hedge_gifts.description: You may carve a simple thorn-mark (three scratches) into a threshold (a door, a gate, a window) while speaking the name of a debtor. For the next day, any attempt by that debtor to cross the threshold without fulfilling their obligation suffers –1 die to all actions.

hedge_gifts.name: The Spoken Clause
hedge_gifts.description: Once per scene, when negotiating a deal, name a previously overlooked term before the deal is accepted. The target may test Resolve (DV 4) to resist the clause's supernatural persuasion; on a failure, they accept it. The clause must be stated and understood, cannot be added retroactively, and cannot be malicious (e.g., 'you owe me your soul'), though it can be disadvantageous (e.g., 'you will pay double if you fail').

monastic_tradition.name: The Way of the Hag's Bargain
monastic_tradition.description: Monks of the Hag's Bargain learn to recite terms without softening them and to hear a refusal without bargaining past it. They preserve agreements, expose concealed clauses in other people's contracts, and insist that anyone asked to promise knows what will come due.
monastic_tradition.prerequisites: Spirit 3+, Presence 2+, Rite of the Unfinished Promise or Cantor of Morag.
monastic_tradition.quote: A refusal heard clearly is a bargain honestly ended.
monastic_tradition.debt_resistant_frame: Morag states her terms completely; her monks expect the same of other powers. Monks of the Hag's Bargain gain +1 die to resist any magical contract or obligation by finding the hidden clause or unspoken cost. If they succeed, the creditor's terms are revealed to be flawed, and the obligation is reduced by one tier.

basic.name: Unfinished Promise
basic.effect: State a bargain and its escape clause so all parties understand them before acceptance. Gain +1 die when the other party acts to fulfill their obligation; you may invoke the agreed escape clause when its stated condition is met.

advanced.name: Speaking Knot
advanced.effect: Bind a promise with fae knots that tighten when broken. Both parties gain +1 die while keeping the bargain; breaking it escalates consequences (Harm 1, then Harm 2, then Curse).

master.name: Hag's Court
master.effect: Once per session, arbitrate any bargain; state your terms before acceptance; they bind all parties who accept. You may also find and exploit one hidden clause in a binding contract or oath, reducing or redirecting its obligation.
master.cost: After the scene, you gain a permanent Bargain Scar (a faint thorn-mark on your tongue). You may ignore one obligation that would require you to keep a bargain you did not fully understand—the Hag's memory of the deal is sufficient.

monastic_tradition.corruption_note: Monks follow the patron's general Corruption track; the monastic path does not add a second one. Where a tradition needs its own, it must differ from the general track in kind, not degree.

corruption.benefit: Faerie Sight: +1 die to Notice hidden obligations or unspoken costs.
corruption.cost: Bargain Sensitivity: –1 die when refusing offers or walking away; the urge to negotiate bites.

corruption.benefit: Cunning Exchange: Once/scene, propose a trade where you gain equal or greater value for lesser seeming payment.
corruption.cost: Debt Awareness: Ever-counting ledgers of owed/owing; suffer Fatigue 1 in crowded markets.

corruption.benefit: Old-Road Wisdom: +2 dice when dealing with spirits, fae, or ancient powers.
corruption.cost: Obligation Magnet: 'Fair trades' find you, each with an explicit cost you are tempted to accept.

corruption.benefit: Bargain Mastery: Once/session, set terms so favorable that even the other party feels satisfied (for now).
corruption.cost: Price Collector: Collect on at least one outstanding debt each session or suffer –1 die to social rolls.

corruption.benefit: Crossroads Power: Once/session, call on a crossroads where you bargained before.
corruption.cost: Fate Entanglement: Your pacts snag your circles; –1 die to keep agreements purely personal.

corruption.benefit: Hag's Court: Once/session, arbitrate any bargain; your stated terms bind all parties who accept.
corruption.cost: Debt Incarnate: Mark +3 Obligation; risk becoming a walking covenant, unable to act without minting new debts.

playstyle_notes.description:
Morag rewards the player who listens to what was actually said. She keeps every promise exactly, warns honestly and only once, and never twists a bargain out of malice — the thorn in the rose is real, it is not hidden, and finding it was the character's job.

Play her without relish. She should never gloat, never bargain twice for the same thing, and never seem pleased when a cost lands. Her intrusions are an old kindness coming back around, or a clause the table forgot and she did not. Tables that dislike 'gotcha' patrons usually love Morag once they work out she has never once cheated anybody, and that the harshness and the fairness are the same quality seen from two sides.
emphasizes: Faerie Bargaining: strict forms, stated costs, and a real opportunity to refuse
Exact Terms: remember what was agreed after it becomes inconvenient
Hearth-Way Wisdom: spirits, thresholds, and difficult remedies
Consequential Magic: boons that demand agreed upkeep
Cruel Precision: promises kept without softening their consequences

sample_adventure.title: The Price Spoken Once
sample_adventure.description: A village elder bought a generation of peace from Morag by promising the orchard at its end. The surviving witnesses remember the terms; the families who planted new trees there were never told. Morag has come for what was promised. The party can challenge the elder's authority to pledge other people's land, seek a substitute Morag will accept, or help the village surrender the orchard. Concealing the cost was the elder's act, and finding the agreement will not make that cost easier to bear.
sample_adventure.quote: I told him what I would take. Ask him what he told you.

guises.name: The Kettle-Crone
guises.note: An extra bowl is put beside the stove when someone intends to seek her. The person can eat before deciding. Morag's hospitality and the bargain that follows are different acts, and the food need not be made sinister to make the terms dreadful. A house that warns its visitor properly may still be hoping they will say yes.

guises.name: The Crossroads Wife
guises.note: She receives a title appropriate to a respectable married woman and a seat slightly apart from the household saints. Petitioners come when law, kinship, and available money have failed to produce what they need. A local broker may arrange the meeting, but Morag states the terms herself. A broker promising a kinder private interpretation is the unreliable party.

guises.name: The Tide-Mother
guises.note: Smuggling households address her before asking for concealment, passage, or someone returned. The maritime title also belongs to Raéyn in other regions. Zakov's keepers distinguish a bargain with the woman by the cauldron from the moods of the sea. A traveler who confuses them may arrive prepared for a libation when a decision is required.

guises.name: The Wife at the Last Hearth
guises.note: She is spoken of where ordinary hospitality has been exhausted. A family may remember who went to her before the birth of its oldest living member and decline to repeat the terms in front of a guest. That reserve protects the family's privacy; it does not mean Morag withheld the cost from the person who accepted it.

provenance.origin: Her names have accumulated around meetings whose locations seldom remain useful directions to the next petitioner.
provenance.summary: Aelaerem accounts often begin with a meal; Viterran accounts with a petition nobody else would hear; Zakov stories with a boat returning where no boat should have reached. Later tellers like to introduce a clever concealed clause. The Tarnished Cauldron's keepers object to those versions. They insist the frightening part was that the petitioner heard the cost plainly and accepted it anyway.
provenance.the_migration: The cult traveled through returned petitioners and households affected by their bargains. A family carrying a gift into a new region might preserve Morag's old title long after it no longer described the local country. Neighbors adopted the title, a meeting custom, or the practice of having the terms repeated before witnesses. Morag herself does not need to have followed the same road as the people who learned to ask for her.
provenance.why_it_took: Intermediaries grew influential because need is often private. Some helped people understand an offer without deciding for them. Others learned exactly whom to bring to the crossroads and which ordinary remedy to leave unmentioned. They do not have to falsify Morag's words to exploit a desperate person. The existence of her honest bargain can support a thoroughly dishonest business around access to it.
provenance.note: Mab, Inaea, and Morag should remain distinct. Mab arranges true statements within inescapable courtesy; Inaea arranges enduring relationships. Morag names what will be taken. Her terms are not made harmless by being clear, and a mortal agent's misconduct does not imply that Morag lied.

philosophy.name: Knowing What You Agree To
philosophy.summary: A stated cost permits an informed decision. It does not make every available decision fair, nor make a desperate person free of the circumstances that brought them.
philosophy.the_point: Her followers divide over what a witness owes the petitioner. One repeats the terms exactly and considers the task complete. Another asks whether someone could help without the bargain. Morag can tolerate the question more easily than the intermediary whose standing depends on the meeting.
philosophy.the_third_thing: The ordeal belongs to the accepted loss and the person who must live after receiving the gift. A hidden extra price usually weakens it by letting the petitioner become only a victim of deceit.
philosophy.at_the_table: Make the terms and the desired outcome clear before acceptance. Give the party an ordinary alternative that is genuinely difficult, not secretly impossible. Honor a refusal. Once a bargain is accepted, let its actual consequences carry the horror rather than adding a clause afterward.
